title: Ada and the Well
premise: Gideon Quintana, a hospice nurse who hears the dying count backwards and documents everything as a form of prayer, takes a post at a crumbling estate in the village of Hollowmere, where the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings each night at the hour of an unrecorded drowning. The Quintana family, who inherited the well on the property through a deed no one can explain, are being drawn into the count themselves: one by one they begin counting backwards in their sleep. Gideon must uncover the 1911 crime the bell keeps tolling for—a girl named Ada pushed into the well by the family whose heirs now live there—and get the family to renounce the inheritance before the last resident signs the papers that would bind them all to Ada's fate. In the end, Gideon burns the deed at the well's mouth; the bell falls silent mid-stroke, but Gideon's notebook fills, page after page, with a backward count in handwriting that is not their own.
about_author: Freya Winterbourne is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing drowned-village records along the Welsh marches before turning to fiction. She writes horror about paperwork, bells, and the debts families refuse to acknowledge.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. At the hospice, Gideon documents Mrs. Aldous counting backwards from forty to zero, dying precisely at one. The emotional beat is quiet dread: Gideon treats documentation as prayer, but this entry feels like a summons rather than a record.

chapters.title: Hollowmere
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Gideon arrives at the Quintana estate as live-in nurse for matriarch Rosa, finding a village that won't look at the house and a dry stone well roped off like a grave. Beat: unease dressed up as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. At midnight the church bell rings; the vicar insists it was melted down in 1911 and sold for scrap. The whole Quintana family stands in the yard listening. Beat: collective denial cracking open.

chapters.title: Rosa's Papers
chapters.summary: POV Rosa. The dying matriarch reviews the family deed to the well, which predates the house itself and names 'Ada' as grantor. She hides it from her children. Beat: guilt disguised as prudence.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. A second hospice patient, unrelated to the family, counts backwards and whispers 'she's still down there.' Gideon cross-references old parish registers. Beat: the horror becomes historical.

chapters.title: Ada, 1911
chapters.summary: POV interleaved diary fragments. The found diary of a scullery maid describes Ada, a servant girl, and the well the household used for 'quiet problems.' Beat: sympathy for the dead, suspicion of the living ancestors.

chapters.title: The First to Count
chapters.summary: POV Marisol, Rosa's granddaughter. Marisol wakes counting backwards from thirty-nine and cannot stop until dawn. Her brother calls it stress. Beat: terror of losing ownership of your own mouth.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Gideon's meticulous notes begin showing entries they don't remember writing, all describing the well. Beat: the archivist realizes the archive is writing back.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. The elderly vicar reveals the 1911 drowning was hushed up by the founding family—the Quintanas' forebears—and the bell was melted so it could never toll the hour again. Beat: justice deferred for a century.

chapters.title: Renounce It
chapters.summary: POV Tomas, Rosa's son. Gideon urges the family to legally renounce the inheritance; Tomas refuses—the land is their livelihood and their name. Beat: greed and legacy versus survival.

chapters.title: Thirty-Eight Nights
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Each night the count starts lower; Marisol's cousin begins counting too. The family stops sleeping in shifts and starts sleeping together like frightened animals. Beat: siege mentality.

chapters.title: The Well Breathes
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Descending the roped-off shaft with a lamp, Gideon finds water where surveys say there is none, and hears a child humming above them. Beat: awe curdling into violation.

chapters.title: Sign Here
chapters.summary: POV Rosa. A solicitor arrives uninvited with papers transferring full title of the well to Rosa alone; she signs with a hand that isn't quite hers. Beat: the trap closing through legal language.

chapters.title: The Hour of the Melted Bell
chapters.summary: POV Tomas. The bell rings thirteen times; every Quintana counts aloud in unison without waking. Tomas records it on his phone; playback is only the sound of water. Beat: helplessness before evidence that erases itself.

chapters.title: What Gideon Buried
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Flashback: years ago Gideon ignored a dying man's backwards count and the man's daughter drowned herself at the same hour. Gideon's documentation has always been penance. Beat: the witness becomes the accused.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: POV Rosa. Rosa, failing fast, is moved to the hospice wing; the staff call her 'the last resident.' She tells Gideon where the original 1911 verdict is hidden—in the bell's salvaged clapper, kept as a mantelpiece ornament. Beat: confession at the threshold.

chapters.title: Clapper
chapters.summary: POV Gideon and Marisol. They break open the clapper and find the coroner's suppressed verdict naming Rosa's grandfather as Ada's killer. Beat: justice outside the law, finally written down.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud at Midnight
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. The family reads the verdict over the open well; the count pauses at eleven for the first time in weeks. Then the papers Rosa signed ignite on the mantel untouched. Beat: hope that costs something.

chapters.title: Before the Last Signature
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Rosa, dying, must sign a formal renunciation—but her hand only writes numbers. Gideon guides it stroke by stroke, praying in ink. Beat: tenderness under extremity.

chapters.title: Zero
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Rosa reaches the end of her count and dies at dawn as the bell rings one final time; the renunciation holds, and the well's water drains away audibly, like a held breath released. Beat: grief and release entwined.

chapters.title: The Deed in the Fire
chapters.summary: POV Tomas. Tomas burns the original deed at the well's mouth against his own instincts, weeping for the name he is giving up. The rope around the well crumbles to rust. Beat: inheritance refused as salvation.

chapters.title: A New Entry
chapters.summary: POV Gideon, epilogue. Months later, Gideon's notebook fills overnight with a backward count in a child's handwriting, ending at one. In the margin, small and clear: 'thank you.' Beat: peace that remains, unmistakably, a haunting.
